patch.description_medium: On March 30, 2017, Senators Sherrod Brown, Ben Cardin and Dianne Feinstein asked federal officials to investigate the Trump Organization’s Azerbaijan dealings. Their letter raised questions about anti-corruption compliance and possible Iran-sanctions violations involving Trump Tower Baku and its partners. It requested scrutiny rather than announcing an investigation or establishing a violation.
patch.description_long:
On March 30, 2017, Senate Democrats Sherrod Brown, Ben Cardin and Dianne Feinstein wrote to Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, Attorney General Jeff Sessions and FBI Director James Comey about the Trump Organization’s Baku project. Their concerns followed a New Yorker investigation into the company’s relationship with Azerbaijan’s Mammadov family and alleged connections to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The senators asked the Justice Department to examine whether the company had conducted adequate due diligence under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and whether it had ignored warning signs about its partners. They asked Treasury to assess sanctions compliance, including the possibility that project-related payments involved an IRGC-linked construction firm. Although the company had reportedly withdrawn from the project, the letter argued that questions about earlier conduct remained. These were allegations and requests for agency action. The letter did not itself establish criminal liability, show that investigators opened a case, or report an enforcement outcome.
patch.corrected_wording: Correction proposed: identify the letter’s authors as Sherrod Brown, Ben Cardin and Dianne Feinstein. The preliminary proposal and supplied context named the wrong senators.

evidence_notes: Coordinator opened the supplied Senate release, which reproduces the full March 30 letter. Corrected names and developed supported procedural context; unknown investigation outcome does not block this account.

patch.description_medium: On July 1, 2021, New York prosecutors announced charges against Trump Corporation, Trump Payroll Corporation and CFO Allen Weisselberg over an alleged compensation-tax scheme. The attorney general said Weisselberg failed to pay taxes on approximately $1.7 million in compensation. The indictment accused the businesses and executive; it did not charge Donald Trump personally.
patch.description_long:
New York prosecutors announced a criminal indictment of Trump Corporation, Trump Payroll Corporation and their chief financial officer, Allen Weisselberg, on July 1, 2021. The two corporate entities operated as part of the Trump Organization. Attorney General Letitia James described the charges as a milestone in a continuing investigation conducted with Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance Jr.

The central allegation was that compensation had been handled in ways that avoided tax reporting and payment. Prosecutors said Weisselberg failed to pay state and federal income taxes on approximately $1.7 million in benefits. The indictment identified apartment rent, car payments and school tuition among the alleged off-the-books compensation. The case therefore concerned how employee benefits were recorded and taxed, alongside the responsibilities of the companies paying them. Donald Trump was not a defendant in this indictment. At this stage the charges remained accusations, and the defendants were presumed innocent; later pleas or verdicts are separate developments.

evidence_notes: Coordinator read Attorney General July 1 statement and contemporaneous full-indictment report. Added event-specific scheme facts and procedural context while keeping allegations distinct from later outcomes.
